title: dLoRA: Dynamically Orchestrating Requests and Adapters for LoRA LLM Serving
technique: Dynamic merge/unmerge of LoRA adapters with base model via credit-based batching, plus request-adapter co-migration (ILP-derived heuristic) across replicas

optimized_metrics.evidence: Based on the request arrival pattern and current state, dLoRA dynamically switches between merged and unmerged inference with different batching strategies to reduce the end-to-end latency.
optimized_metrics.stat_quote: We use the average latency as the primary metric to evaluate the performance of dLoRA

optimized_metrics.evidence: The goal of the migration algorithm is to minimize the overall running time among all replicas.
Starvation prevention. Although dynamic batching accelerates LoRA LLM serving, it may cause starvation.

headline_claim.text: dLoRA improves the throughput by up to 57.9× and 26.0×, compared to vLLM and HugginFace PEFT, respectively. Compared to the concurrent work S-LoRA, dLoRA achieves up to 1.8× lower average latency.

reported_metrics.where: Figs 9-12 average latency (s/token) vs request rate
Figs 9-11 max throughput under the latency SLO (0.5 s)
§7.3 queueing delay of requests as load-imbalance indicator

metric_definitions.definition_quote: We use the average latency as the primary metric to evaluate the performance of dLoRA. Following prior work on LLM serving [11, 12], the average latency is calculated by dividing the sum of each request's end-to-end latency by the total number of output tokens.
metric_definitions.notes: ratio of sum E2E to sum of output tokens (token-weighted), not mean of per-request normalized latency; Fig axes in s/token

metric_definitions.term_as_written: latency SLO / max throughput under SLO
metric_definitions.definition_quote: we set a latency service level objective (SLO) and compare the maximum throughput achieved by each system under the SLO. Similar to prior work, we set the latency SLO to 10× of the latency of a single iteration in the decoding phase. Specifically, SLO is 0.5 seconds based on our profiling.
metric_definitions.notes: SLO applied to average latency (s/token) curve, not to per-request attainment; throughput = max request rate at which average latency <= SLO; units of throughput (req/s) not strictly defined

metric_definitions.term_as_written: peak capacity of a LoRA adapter
metric_definitions.definition_quote: we define the peak capacity of a LoRA adapter as the number of requests that can be served by the unallocated GPU memory where the corresponding LoRA adapter resides.
The goal of the migration algorithm is to minimize the overall running time among all replicas.
metric_definitions.notes: re-pass: ILP objective over the current requests/adapters placement; batch wall-clock, not per-request latency

slo_spec: Latency SLO = 10x the latency of one decode iteration = 0.5 s (average latency in s/token) from profiling; max throughput at that SLO compared
load_regime: request-rate sweep on Azure production traces (rescaled), varied skewness and scale ratio, numbers of adapters (up to 128)
tradeoff_acknowledged: Dynamic merge/unmerge may preempt some requests (switching overhead); credit-based mechanism prevents starvation; paper reports P90 still improved
hardware: 4 nodes x 8 NVIDIA A800 80GB (32 GPUs), 200 Gbps InfiniBand
workloads: Microsoft Azure Functions traces 2019 (MAF1) and 2021 (MAF2) used as request arrival patterns
extractor_notes: Primary metric is mean latency normalized by total output tokens (s/token), SLO of 0.5 s defined on that average, so 'throughput under SLO' is capacity at a mean-latency threshold, not goodput in the DistServe sense. Only P90 reported as a tail stat (Fig 10b). Source: USENIX open-access PDF (no arXiv).
